overview: Wurundjeri people connect Birrarung and surrounding Country through language, family, leadership and skilled work. Greenstone quarrying, William Barak's drawings and community canoe building reveal different ways of making and sharing knowledge. Colonial dispossession changed access to land, but Wurundjeri identity and cultural responsibilities continue.

periods.title: Coranderrk and the struggle to retain land
periods.summary: Wonga and Barak helped establish Coranderrk in 1863. Barak's leadership, petitions and pictures became important records of community life during colonial dispossession. Later descendants carried those relationships forward.

periods.title: Community organization and cultural renewal
periods.summary: Wurundjeri descendants established their corporation in 1985. Later returns of land, canoe making and Birrarung advocacy brought cultural responsibilities into new public institutions and projects.

items.text: At Wil-im-ee Moor-ring, Mount William, quarry pits, waste stone and working areas preserve the remains of greenstone tool production. Makers shaped rough hatchet heads at the quarry; recipients could then grind and finish them for their own needs.

Hatchets supported canoe building, food gathering and the manufacture of wooden implements. Mount William greenstone travelled through exchange: visitors brought goods including possum-skin cloaks and spears. The quarry therefore connects household work with relationships between communities.

In the 1880s, William Barak described quarry access to Alfred Howitt. His account identifies Billibellary as a custodian approached through messengers. It adds evidence of authority and negotiated access to the physical traces of stoneworking.

Barak's Untitled drawing of 1899, now in the National Gallery of Victoria, uses pencil and watercolor to show a ceremonial gathering. An inscription on its calico wrapping dates the gift to Annie Danks to January 1899, giving the work a documented personal history.

The drawing includes possum-skin cloaks, feather headdresses, boomerangs used as clapsticks, fires and animals. These details communicate clothing, movement and performance through an artist's composition; the image is a cultural account, not a complete inventory of every Wurundjeri ceremony.

Simon Wonga and William Barak helped establish Coranderrk in 1863 for Wurundjeri and other displaced Kulin people. They sought space for a community amid colonial dispossession. The station provided a place to live, but its administration constrained people's control over their land.

Barak became Ngurungaeta after Wonga's death in 1874. His petitions to retain Coranderrk show leadership exercised through negotiation and written advocacy, alongside the cultural knowledge communicated in his pictures.

In the 2012 Kooroong project, community members worked greenstone into axes and used them to remove bark from a river red gum at Plenty Gorge for a canoe. The project brought stoneworking, tree knowledge and boat construction together in a living practice.

Wurundjeri accounts treat landforms and habitats as integral parts of cultural heritage. Care for Country includes relationships and continuing practices, as well as protecting individual sites or objects.

Descendants established the Wurundjeri corporation in 1985. The return of part of Coranderrk, including its cemetery, in March 1998 restored a connection to a place with deep family significance, without undoing every earlier loss.

Land titles for Wil-im-ee Moor-ring and the Sunbury Rings returned in 2012. In 2017, Elders addressed Victoria's Parliament as part of advocacy for Birrarung. These events show cultural authority expressed through landholding and public decision-making.

ending.text: Wurundjeri people continue despite dispossession and reserve controls. Coranderrk belongs to that history, but does not define its beginning or end. Descendants sustain leadership, artistic knowledge and responsibilities to Birrarung and Country through family life and community institutions.
